sections.label: Note
paragraphs: You may put it in a scenario for compatibility. It never blocks anyone.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In the original game this ended the script when the scenario had not been registered. In this game registered behaviour applies, so the code does nothing and the script goes on to the next action.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: Like code 98, it never blocks anyone.

codes.title: End a battle and give out rewards

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: The reward kind. The game doubles it before use.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Closes the battle from a script and goes through the reward flow that the ID chooses. The land is reloaded. The script then goes on to the next action, after the reward windows have been closed.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

The ID decides how the end of the battle is handled. 0 is the ordinary reward flow, with treasure and victory points. 1 only asks which survivors are kept and hands out no treasure or victory points. 5 recovers loot. If the squad has fled or fallen, every kind other than 1 and 5 is handled like 1.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: The enemy count is brought up to the number of monsters met, so the battle counts as won. The last-picture marker is reset, which makes the next picture be drawn fresh.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A guard captain's script finishes with code 100 and ID 0 after he surrenders, so the squad collects its reward without killing the rest of the garrison.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: Only 0, 1 and 5 have been checked. Test any other ID before relying on it.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Puts the squad back on the square it came from, redraws the map and ends the script.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: It works anywhere, in towns and dungeons alike. Nothing after it in the script runs.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A toll bridge guard turns the squad away when it has no pass. The script tests for the pass and runs code 101 when the test fails.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Sets the victory points still to be earned by each picked warrior to 1, marks every warrior active, and then runs the ordinary reward flow. The points are then shared out as a reward.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: The 1 is a total to divide, not "one level". One warrior receiving it gets 1 point. Two receiving it get 0 each, because the whole number share is 0.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: After a shrine blessing, pick the warrior who prayed and run this code to bring his next promotion within reach.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Lets the script go on only if the squad is, or is not, in a boat and camping, and can put the squad in the boat or take it out.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Boat test.
2) Camping test.
3) Set the boat.
4) Not used.
5) Not used.
1) 1 needs the squad to be in a boat. 2 needs it not to be in a boat. 0 does not test.
2) 1 needs the squad to be camping. 2 needs it not to be. 0 does not test.
3) 1 puts the squad in a boat. 2 takes it out. 0 leaves it as it is. The map is redrawn when this changes.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: When a test fails the script ends, but E3 is still applied first, because the tests and the setting are done in the same step.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A ferryman scene uses E1 = 2 and E3 = 1: it only runs on land and then puts the squad on the boat.

codes.title: Turn random battles on or off

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: 1 allows random battles. 0 stops them.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Controls whether random-encounter rectangles can start battles.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: The value is kept as one byte, so IDs above 255 wrap around.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: Put ID 0 on the entry square of a safe town. Put ID 1 on its gate.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: 0 lets held-over allies take part. Any other value suspends them.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: While allies are suspended they do not fight alongside the squad and they do not join the reward and survivor choices after a battle.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: Use 1 to suspend and 0 to bring the allies back. This setting is not part of the allies themselves, so they come back unchanged.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: The squad must cross a narrow ledge on its own. Use ID 1 at the foot of the ledge and ID 0 at the top.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Makes the current land light or dark and redraws it.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Light level.
2) Stop if unchanged.
1) 1 is light. 2 is dark.
2) Any value other than 0 ends the script when the land already has that level, so the change and its text do not repeat each time the squad steps there.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: Only these two E-Codes are read.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A cave mouth sets E1 = 2 and E2 = 1 so that the lights go out once, the first time the squad enters.

codes.title: Battle with a choice of battles

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Plays a sound and a text, fights one battle chosen by the script, and returns the squad to the land. If the squad retreats or loses, a script of your choice runs from its first action.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Battle number, or the first of a range.
2) Last of a range.
3) Sound number.
4) Text number.
5) Script to run when the battle was not won.
1) The battle to fight.
2) 0 fights E1. Any other value picks a battle at random from E1 up to E2.
3) 0 plays nothing.
4) 0 shows nothing. The text is shown before the fight and does not wait for a click.
5) The script number. It runs only when the squad retreated or lost. If the squad wins, the land is reloaded and the ordinary rewards are given.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: Every warrior is marked active afterward.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A swamp ambush with E1 = 12, E2 = 15, E3 = 300 and E5 = 88: a random battle from 12 to 15, and script 88 if the squad flees.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Adds a number to one statistic of every picked warrior. Each warrior's screen is refreshed afterward.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Which statistic.
2) Amount to add.

1) The statistic:
1 = actions per round (minimum 0).
2 = scans per battle (minimum 1; skipped if the warrior has none).
3 = movement per round (minimum 3).
4 = bare-hand minimum damage (minimum 0).
5 = most psi (minimum 0; skipped if the warrior has none).
6 = bare-hand maximum damage (minimum 1; skipped if it is 0).
7 = most stamina (minimum 2).
8 = armor (minimum 0).
9 = melee accuracy bonus (minimum 0).
10 = missile accuracy bonus (minimum 0).
11 = psi resistance bonus (minimum 0).
Any other value does nothing.
2) May be negative. A result below the minimum becomes the minimum.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: For movement, psi and stamina the current value is also pulled down when it ends up above the new most. It is not raised.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A cursed spring: E1 = 7, E2 = -5 lowers every picked warrior's greatest stamina by 5.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: The amount, a whole number. It may be negative.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Adds the amount to the mission score kept with the game.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: The score is a 16-bit signed number and wraps at its limits.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: No other effect of the score was confirmed. Test this in your scenario before relying on it.

codes.title: Go to the next stage of the mission

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: The stage, counted from 1, with a sign. The stage is the ID without its sign: 1 or -1 is the first stage. A positive ID asks the player to confirm. A negative ID goes straight on. Do not use 0, which names no stage.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Moves the squad to a new stage of the mission: the stage name is shown, the squad appears at the stage's starting land and square, and the stage's opening movie plays.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: A positive ID first asks a yes or no question. If the player says no, the map is redrawn and the script ends.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.
Its starting land, position and optional starting script come from the scenario's stage record for that stage (stage 1 is the first record). If the stage has a starting script, it runs next.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: Stamina and psi are restored to the most for every warrior except the last one in the squad. Allies held over are let go. The opening movie is the one numbered 1000 plus the stage counted from 0, so stage 1 plays movie 1000 and stage 3 plays movie 1002.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: After the last vault is opened, ID 3 asks "go on?" and, on yes, starts the third stage of the mission with movie 1002.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: Test this in your scenario before relying on it, particularly the restoration of the last warrior.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Opens either a treasure with a limit, or a shop under restricted terms, depending on E1.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Treasure or shop.
2) Limit.
3) Limit mode.
1) A number above 0 is a treasure record. Zero or a negative number is a shop, and the shop number is the number without its sign.
2) A limit the treasure or shop uses (see E-Code 3).
3) The game stores E-Code 3 plus 1 and E-Code 2 as they stand, and opening a shop with Code 6 resets both to 0; what they limit was not confirmed. -1 gives the same stored value as an ordinary shop.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: A treasure runs the ordinary reward windows with the limit set. A shop loops between its window and the pack window until the player leaves, and the script then goes on.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A merchant's stall: Extra Codes 30 holds -7, 0, -1, so shop 7 opens under this code, and the script goes on when the player leaves.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: The exact effect of the limit and its mode on the player's own packs was not confirmed. Test this in your scenario before relying on it.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: The picture number, a whole number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Stores a number as the map picture and redraws the map.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: When the number is 0 the map draws the squad's marker as usual. A different number stops the marker from being drawn as usual.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: What replaces the marker was not confirmed. Test this in your scenario before relying on it.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Used in a monster's script. If every warrior of the squad has fallen, each warrior is restored to 1 stamina and taken off computer control, the fallen count is cleared, and the script and the battle end. Otherwise the monster whose script this is returns to 1 stamina, becomes neutral, and is marked so that scans pass it over.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A healer monster saves the squad from a total defeat: when the squad falls, its death script runs code 119.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: The effect of the scan mark was not confirmed. Test this in your scenario before relying on it.

codes.title: Replace the monster in the battle

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In a battle, changes the selected monster into another kind, or removes it.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) New monster record.
2) Not used.
3) Sound.
4) Text before.
5) Text after.
1) The monster record number to put in place. -1 removes the monster: its body is killed and the script ends.
3) 0 plays nothing.
4) 0 shows nothing. The text is shown first, with the view centred on the monster.
5) 0 shows nothing. The text is shown after the change.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: The replacement keeps the old monster's side. If the new monster has a different size from the old one, the monster is not replaced and the script ends, but the old monster's own script chance has already been turned negative and the text before has been shown. A successful change builds the replacement fresh, plays the sound, and centres the view again.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A werewolf script with E1 = 41 (the beast form), E3 = 530 and E5 = the transformation text.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: Test this in your scenario to see which monster counts as the selected one when the script runs from a death or from a round.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In a battle, destroys every monster that belongs to all of the creature categories named.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Category.
2) Category.
3) Category.
4) Category.
5) Category.

Each is a creature category number, as set on the monster's record. 0 means the entry is not used. A monster is destroyed only when it has every category named. Category 4 is Mechanical. The game does not check the numbers, so use only categories your monster records define. A list of all zeros names no category, so it destroys every monster.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: Every monster in the battle is tested, whether it is an enemy or not and whether it is alive or not. Each destroyed monster leaves with its usual result line and sound.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A banishing relic with E1 = 4 destroys all Mechanical monsters on the field.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In a battle, every living monster of one kind that is on a side stops being an enemy, and counts as defeated.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Monster number.
2) Reverse.
1) The monster number to look for.
2) 0 acts on monsters that are still enemies. Any other value acts on monsters that are already neutral and takes them back off the defeated count.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: In reverse mode the monsters stay neutral. They do not become enemies again. Only the defeated count goes down.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A parley text turns the goblins of monster number 20 into onlookers: E1 = 20, E2 = 0.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In a battle, makes the listed kinds of monsters turn and flee, if they are on the same side as the monster whose script is running.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: 1) to 5) Monster numbers. 0 means the entry is not used.
Each monster of a listed number on the same side as the current monster is set to retreat, and its chance to surrender is set to 70 percent.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: When the chieftain dies, his script routs the warriors of numbers 14 and 15.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In a battle, adds monsters beside the current monster, with the appearing effect.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Not used.
2) Monster record number.
3) How many.
4) Sound.
5) Not used.
2) The monster record to build.
3) A negative number is a random count from 1 up to the number without its sign, drawn each time the step runs.
4) 0 plays nothing. The sound is played for each monster.

Each new monster is placed in the nearest free squares around the current monster, inside the playing field and not on solid ground. The side a new monster takes depends on what started the script: for some scripts it takes the side of the monster whose script is running, and in a round script it keeps the side its own record gives. A battle holds at most 100 monsters. If the roster is already full nothing is added. Do not ask for more monsters than the roster has room for.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A summoner's script with E2 = 8, E3 = 3 and E4 = 410 adds 3 skeletons with a sound each.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: Test this in your scenario before relying on the side the new monsters take.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: In a battle, destroys living monsters of one kind, nearest first.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Monster number.
2) How many.
3) Distance.
1) The monster number to destroy.
2) 0 means up to 999. A negative number is a random count from 1 up to the number without its sign.

3) The furthest distance to look, measured from the monster that fell last. 0 means no limit in practice. Only monsters closer than this distance are destroyed, so 6 reaches monsters up to 5 squares away.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: The side of the monster is not considered, so allies of the same number are destroyed as well.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A purge spell script with E1 = 33, E2 = 2, E3 = 6 destroys up to 2 monsters of number 33 that are less than 6 squares from the fallen monster, nearest first.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: The starting point was only partly confirmed. Test this in your scenario.

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Used inside a battle's round script. It tests whether to switch to another script, and if so it runs the other script from its first action.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Kind of test.
2) Round or percent.
3) Repeat.
4) Script.
5) Last script of a range.
1) 0 passes once the battle is past round E2. 1 passes by chance: a percent roll is made and the step passes if the roll is not above E2. Any other value always passes.
2) The round number for kind 0, or the percent for kind 1.

3) 1 keeps the round script that holds this step, so it is tried again each round. Any other value clears that script once the step passes, so it does not come back. With 2 the new script is chosen at random from E4 to E5. With any other value E4 alone is used.
4) The script to run. With repeat 2 it is the first of the range.
5) The last of the range, read only when E3 is 2.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: When the test is not passed, which is a kind 0 test before the round is past E2 or a kind 1 roll above E2, the script ends at once. A kind 1 test never clears the script.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: E1 = 0, E2 = 4, E3 = 0, E4 = 90: from the fifth round on, script 90 takes over once.

codes.title: Continue if a monster is present

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: A monster number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: The script goes on only if a living monster of that number is in the battle. Otherwise the script ends.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: Note
paragraphs: It reads the monster number itself, not an Extra Codes record.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A mourning scene shown only if the old dragon, monster 77, is still alive.

codes.title: Show an animation on the map

sections.label: ID
paragraphs: An Extra Codes number.

sections.label: Use
paragraphs: Plays a short animation on the outdoor map, centred on one square.

sections.label: Options
paragraphs: None.

sections.label: E-Codes
paragraphs:
1) Animation number.
2) Column on the map.
3) Row on the map.
4) Size.
5) Delay between frames.
1) The animation. Each one has eight frames.
2) and 3) Map squares of the current land.
4) The size of the effect: the side of a square, in pixels (a map square is 32 pixels wide). The square is centred on the top-left corner of the chosen map square.
5) A delay between frames.

sections.label: Example
paragraphs: A lightning strike on the tower: E1 = 2, E2 = 18, E3 = 6, E4 = 64, E5 = 2.

sections.label: Caution
paragraphs: The direction of the column and row and the unit of the delay were not fully confirmed. Test this in your scenario before relying on it.

blocks.p: Scripts drive almost everything that happens on the map that is not a plain fight: a door that asks a question, a shopkeeper, a trap, an ambush, a change in the landscape after the squad has done something. You attach a script to an event on the map, to the choices of an encounter, or to a battle. A script is a short list of **steps**. Each event or encounter record holds up to eight of them.
A step is two numbers: a **code** and an **ID**. The code says what to do. The ID says with what: a string number, a count, a battle number, or the number of an **Extra Codes** record.
The game runs a script one step after another, from the first. A step may stop the script, send it to a different step, or send it into a battle or a shop and bring it back afterwards.

Many codes need more than one number. Those codes use their ID to name an Extra Codes record, a row of five numbers that you fill in with the editor. In this manual they are written as E-Codes and numbered 1) to 5). An Extra Codes record can be shared by as many steps as you like. Each code below lists what its five numbers mean, and when the manual says an E-Code is not used you can leave it at 0.

For several codes the sign of the ID changes the behaviour, for example whether a shop window opens at once (Code 6) or a note is shown at once (Code 29). The **Options** line of each code lists those cases.

blocks.t: Numbers the game does not know

blocks.p: Not every number is a code. If a step has a number that the game does not handle, the step is skipped and the script goes on to the next step. Nothing is shown and nothing is reported. The last chapter lists the numbers that do nothing. A typing error in a code number is therefore easy to miss: if a step seems to be ignored, check its number first.

Each code has the same layout. **ID** tells you what to put in the step's ID. **Use** says what the code does. **Options** lists special values. **E-Codes** lists the five numbers, with a numbered paragraph for each one that needs explaining. **Note** warns about side effects, and **Example** shows the code at work. Where an entry says to test something in your scenario before relying on it, the game's behaviour at that point has not been confirmed down to the last detail, and a quick test costs less than a surprise.

chapters.title: If You Know Realmz or Divinity

blocks.p: New Centurions and Realmz share a scripting scaffold, and its scenario scripts will look familiar if you have used Divinity, the Realmz scenario editor. The numbers, the Extra Codes and the layout of a step are the same idea. But the game around them is different, and some things you may rely on are gone. Read this chapter before you port a script or trust an old habit.

This is the biggest change. In Divinity you could make any branching code a "gosub" by entering the code itself as a negative number (-40 instead of 40). The script you branched to would then finish and return to the step after the branch, and Code 111 returned from a gosub while Code 112 dropped a waiting script. New Centurions has none of this.

li: A branch is a one way ticket. The script you branch to does not return.

A negative code does not make a gosub. A step whose code is negative is skipped, and the script goes on to the next step. The only negative codes that do anything are -14, -32 and -12. -14 picks warriors and then inverts the picks (Divinity's manual does not list it); -32 and -12 are new codes of their own, not gosub forms. A negative ID is a different matter: for some codes it is a real option (see "Positive and negative IDs").
Code 112 is skipped.
**Code 111 does not return.** In New Centurions it opens a limited shop or treasure. A ported script that uses 111 to return will open a shop instead.

blocks.p: To share a scene between places, to continue past eight steps, or to come back to where you were, see "Moving Between Scripts".

li: **Action Point.** In Divinity this is a map event that runs a script, and an "X-AP" is a script that other scripts start by number. In New Centurions action points are what a warrior spends in battle on attacks, reloading and putting on items. This manual says **event** for a place on the map that runs a script, and **script** for a script started by number.
**Extra Codes.** The same idea as Divinity's E-Codes: a row of five numbers that a code names with its ID.

blocks.p: These numbers do a different job here than the Divinity code of the same number. Do not carry a script across without checking each one.

li: **73** waits for a short time. In Divinity it opens a shop that accepts only some items.
**102** sets the victory points still to be earned by the picked warriors to 1 and then runs the ordinary reward flow. In Divinity it levels up the picked characters.
**111** opens a limited shop or treasure. In Divinity it returns from a gosub.
**121** destroys every monster that belongs to all the creature categories you name. In Divinity it de-animates lower undead.
**122** makes every living monster of one kind on a side neutral, so that it counts as defeated. In Divinity it causes a fumble.
**125** destroys living monsters of one kind, nearest first. In Divinity it destroys related monsters, and its options differ.
**14** picks warriors in both games, but Divinity's manual says a negative ID limits the pick to warriors who are conscious. Do not count on the sign working the same way; see the entry for Code 14.

blocks.p: Several other codes do the same job in both games but differ in detail. 30 and 31 (the checks) and 120 (change a monster in a battle) take different Extra Codes. 100 (end a battle) uses its ID to choose the kind of reward. 126 (the round script) takes the same five numbers but starts working from a different round. Read the entry of any code you port, even when its name looks the same.

These Divinity codes are skipped, so a script that uses them loses those steps without any message: the temple offer (32, now the clinic at -32), dungeon entry and exit (37), banking (49), the tile-parameter branch (78), turning cleric turning off and on (82 and 83), the compass and look direction codes (93 to 95), the codes that force or allow the 3D view (96 and 97), and the gosub pop (112). New Centurions has no dungeons or 3D view, so there is nothing for the dungeon codes to do.

-12 clears objects from an area of a map. 109 adds to the mission score, 110 starts a stage of the mission, 113 stores a map picture number and 128 plays a map animation. Divinity has none of these. -32 enters the clinic, which takes the place of Divinity's temple offer (code 32).

In Divinity a check against an attribute rolls dice. In New Centurions the attribute checks in Codes 30 and 31 compare the attribute with a number you give; only the special ability test in Code 30 rolls. The Extra Codes also differ. Read the entries for Codes 30 and 31 before you port a check.
Divinity text is fixed. In New Centurions a `^` and a digit in a story text is replaced with a warrior's name when the text is shown. See "Names in text".

If you are used to gosubs, note that there are none (see "If You Know Realmz or Divinity"). Scripts in New Centurions do not call each other and come back. When a step sends the script somewhere else, it stays there. There is no stack of waiting scripts and no "return" step. A step that opens a battle, a shop or a window simply finishes when it is closed, and the script goes on with the next step. The one way back is out of an encounter: Code 34 returns to the script that opened it with Code 4 or Code 5. Once you know that, everything in this chapter is easy: you move a scene along by handing it to the next script, and you share a scene by pointing many places at the same one.

A script is eight steps. A map event holds one script, and so does each choice of an encounter. You can also store scripts by number, to be started by other scripts. A running script has a position: the next of its eight steps.

The game also keeps one saved copy of a script. Code 4 and Code 5 make it when they open an encounter. It holds the eight steps of the script as they stood then, and the position of the step that opened the encounter. Code 34 puts that copy back and carries on with the step after the one that opened the encounter. Only one copy is kept, so a Code 4 or Code 5 run from inside an encounter replaces it. Nothing else about a waiting script is remembered, and no other step goes back to it.

When the last step has run, the script is finished. A step that ends the script by passing the last step (for example Code 42 with E2 = -2) counts as running out of steps. If a map event started the script and no encounter is on screen, the event is then marked as spent: its chance becomes -1, so it does not run again unless Code 13 gives it a chance back. Some steps leave the script at once and do not mark the event: Code 3 with outcome 0, Code 101, a Code 8 whose chance test fails, a Code 20 whose arrival event fails its own chance test, and a battle (Code 2) that the squad loses.

Code 24 ends the script without marking the event, so the squad can trigger it again, and it clears an encounter that is on screen. Jump type 3 of the branch codes below does the same. Code 42 and Codes 58 and 59 with E2 = 2, and Code 75 with E3 = 1, also keep the event, but they do not clear an encounter that is on screen: while it has visits left, it may be shown again.

blocks.t: Handing a scene to another script

blocks.p: The codes that test something and branch each name where the script goes next. Codes 46, 58 and 59 do it with a **branch type**, a **number** and, for encounters, a **start action**:

li: -1 goes straight to the eighth step of this script.
0 starts the script with that number from its first step.
1 and 2 jump into one of the four choices of the simple or the typed encounter that is on screen, starting at the step you give. Steps are counted from 0, so 0 is the first step and 7 is the eighth.
3 ends the script, keeps the event and clears the encounter, like Code 24.

blocks.p: The others (for example 76 and 77) name a script, a simple encounter or a typed encounter directly; each entry lists its values. Every branch is a one way ticket. The old script does not carry on with its remaining steps afterwards. If you want a step to run after the branch, put it in the script you branch to.
Three more codes move a scene without a test:

li: **Code 39** replaces the running script with another one and starts it from its first step. Use it to carry a scene past eight steps: make the eighth step of each script a Code 39 that points at the next.

**Code 8** copies the eight steps of another event on the same map over the running script and starts from the top, after testing the running event's chance again. Use it to make several places share one scene.

**Code 7** rewrites a map event, or one choice of an encounter, so that from now on it runs a different script. The change lasts the rest of the game. Use it when the story changes the world: the bridge is gone, the guard has gone home.

blocks.p: **Example:** Three fountains on one map should all offer the same blessing. Write the blessing once as event 20 on that map, and end it with Code 24. Give each fountain's own event a chance of 100 and a single step, Code 8 with ID 20. When you later improve the blessing, you change event 20 and all three fountains change with it.

blocks.t: Coming back to where you were

blocks.p: Because a branch never returns, a scene that has to pick up where it left off needs a note. Use a mission flag.

1. Before you send the squad away, set a flag with Code 47, or bump a counter with Code 76. 2. In the script you branch to, finish what it needs to do. 3. When the squad comes back, the event that starts the scene tests the flag with Code 46 or Code 77 and goes to the script for the next part.

**Example:** A prisoner scene has two halves, before and after the key. The first script sets flag 14 and sends the squad into the cells. The door event tests flag 14 with Code 46: set, it starts script 61, "the prisoner is freed"; clear, it starts script 60, "the door is locked".
Mission flags are one byte each and Code 76 uses the same ones as counters, so give each purpose its own flag number.

blocks.t: Asking a question and acting on the answer

blocks.p: Code 3 asks the player a question and then does what you chose for the answer: carry on, step the party back, replace the script, jump into an encounter choice, or end. Replacing the script (outcome 1) gives each answer its own scene, and nothing comes back afterwards. See the entry for Code 3.

li: A script is eight steps. For a longer scene, chain scripts with Code 39.

The steps of an encounter's choices keep their code in one signed byte, so a choice can hold codes from -128 to 127 only. Code 128 cannot be used in a choice; use it in a map event or a stored script.

blocks.p: **Caution:** Test Codes 7, 8 and 39 in your scenario when the script that uses them is running from the choice of an encounter on screen. Check what the player sees as the old script is replaced.
If you are bringing a script from Realmz or Divinity, read "If You Know Realmz or Divinity" first. Check every ported script for negative codes and for Code 111 before you play it.

A story text can name your warriors. Put a caret and a digit in the text, and the game replaces both with a warrior's name when the text is shown. The name that is put in is never read again as a token. Do not end a text with a caret.

The digits 1 to 6 stand for the squad's warriors in their order: ^1 is the first warrior, ^2 the second, and so on up to ^6. If the warrior in that place has fallen, the name of the last warrior in the squad who still stands is used instead. If nobody stands, ^1 to ^6 show the name of the warrior in their own place, fallen as that warrior is. For a place past the end of a smaller squad the game is meant to do the same as for a fallen warrior, but that depends on the game's empty warrior records; test it in your scenario.

^0 follows the same rule from the other end: it is meant to give the name of the last warrior who stands. That depends on the game's empty record before the first warrior, so test ^0 in your scenario before relying on it.
^9 names the warrior chosen by the most recent pick, and remembers him.

li: The first text that uses ^9 after a pick takes the picked warrior who stands lowest in the squad (not necessarily the one the player clicked first). Every later text that uses ^9 names the same warrior, until the next pick begins.
A pick begins whenever the game asks the player to choose a warrior: Codes 14, -14 and 31, the choice of a warrior for a Psi action out on the map, and the choice of a warrior to bandage in a battle.
Codes 30, 50, 52 and 53 pick warriors too, but they do not begin a pick for ^9. After one of them, ^9 still names the warrior of the earlier pick.
In an unusual case, when the game's record of the warrior in the ninth place is missing, ^9 is treated like any other digit and shows the name of the last warrior who stands.
If nothing has been picked yet, test ^9 in your scenario before relying on it.

blocks.p: ^7 and ^8 are not meant for scenarios. They give the first warrior's name or the last warrior who stands.

The choices of a simple encounter are not filled in. A choice that contains a token shows the caret and the digit exactly as you wrote them. Put the tokens in the encounter's text, not in its choices.

**Example 1:** The text "^1 tests the rope and ^2 is told to hold it." shows, for a squad of Brutus and Livia, "Brutus tests the rope and Livia is told to hold it." If Livia has fallen, it shows "Brutus tests the rope and Brutus is told to hold it.", because the last warrior standing is Brutus.

**Example 2:** After a party pick of one warrior, the text "^9 pulls the lever." and a later text "^9 curses the stone door." both name the same warrior. If the script picks again, the next text that uses ^9 names the new pick.
**Caution:** Test ^9 in your scenario after a pick before relying on it.
The game skips the numbers below. When a script reaches one of them the step is skipped and the script goes on to the next step. It is not an error, and nothing is shown.

li: 32 (the clinic is Code -32), 37, 49
129 and every number above it
Every negative number except -32, -14 and -12. This includes -1 to -11, -13, -15 to -31 and anything below -32.

blocks.p: Codes 98 and 99 are handled, but they have no effect in the registered game, as their entries describe.
